claims.text: The initial material is a single-phase high-entropy alloy.
The initial alloy has uniformly distributed elements and cohesive, compositionally uniform grain boundaries.
Combined cyclic loading and thermal exposure induce stress-assisted solute nanoclustering at grain boundaries.
Applied stress and thermal energy accelerate local diffusion that produces grain-boundary nanoclusters.
Solute-rich grain-boundary nanoclusters weaken interfacial cohesion.
Weakened grain-boundary cohesion lowers fracture toughness and promotes brittle failure.
The proposed brittle response can occur without conventional grain-boundary segregation or intermetallic precipitation.
After combined loading and thermal treatment, TEM and atom-probe tomography will reveal solute-rich nanoclusters along grain boundaries.
Treatment will reduce ductility and fracture toughness relative to the as-fabricated control.
Nanocluster density will correlate with the severity of mechanical embrittlement.
The as-manufactured baseline alloy has high toughness and ductility.
The mechanism operates from approximately 300 K to 1073 K at strain rates that bracket an embrittlement regime.
Within the applicable regime, grain coarsening and coarse precipitate formation remain suppressed.
The applicable stress and temperature regime is sufficient for nanoclustering but insufficient for large-scale phase separation.
Grain-boundary segregation and grain-boundary second-phase precipitation are established routes to loss of ductility or grain-boundary cracking in alloys.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis denies conventional grain-boundary segregation while defining the mediator as localized enrichment of solutes at grain boundaries, which is itself a form of segregation. The distinction could be coherent if 'conventional segregation' meant equilibrium monolayer-scale segregation rather than clustering, but that distinction is not operationally defined.
